q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a gaseous Cr³⁺ ion (Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹)?
x: Cr³⁺ loses the 4s electron and two 3d electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d³. By Hund's rule the three d electrons occupy separate orbitals, so all 3 are unpaired. Six is the number for the neutral Cr atom.

q: Which gaseous ion has the electronic configuration [Ar] 3d⁸?
x: Nickel is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s²; losing both 4s electrons gives Ni²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁸. Co²⁺ is 3d⁷, Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ and Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹.

q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a gaseous Fe³⁺ ion?
x: Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵ (Fe loses 4s² and one 3d electron). Five d electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly, so all 5 are unpaired. Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) has 4.

q: The electronic configuration of the V²⁺ ion (V, Z = 23) is:
x: Vanadium is [Ar] 3d³ 4s². Forming V²⁺ removes the two 4s electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d³.

q: The electronic configuration of the Cu²⁺ ion is:
x: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Cu²⁺ loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d⁹ with one unpaired electron. [Ar] 3d¹⁰ is Cu⁺.

q: The highest oxidation state shown by manganese (Mn, [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²) is:
x: The maximum oxidation state equals the total number of 3d and 4s electrons that can be used in bonding: 5 + 2 = 7, as in KMnO₄. +2 uses only the 4s electrons.

q: Scandium (Z = 21) shows only the +3 oxidation state in its compounds because:
o: Scandium has no 4s electrons to lose
It loses its electrons from the 3p subshell first
Losing its 3d¹ 4s² electrons gives Sc³⁺ the stable argon configuration
x: Sc is [Ar] 3d¹ 4s². Removing all three outer electrons gives Sc³⁺ with the noble-gas configuration [Ar] (3d⁰), which is very stable, so other oxidation states are not usual.

q: Zinc is not regarded as a typical transition element because:
o: Both the Zn atom and the Zn²⁺ ion have a completely filled 3d subshell
Zinc has no electrons in its 3d subshell
Zinc loses its 3d electrons before its 4s electrons
x: A typical transition element has an incomplete d subshell in the atom or a common ion. Zn is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² and Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, so its d subshell is always full; it shows only the +2 state.

q: Copper atoms have a full 3d¹⁰ subshell, yet copper is counted as a transition element because:
o: Its ion Cu²⁺ has a completely filled 3d subshell
It has electrons in the 4p subshell
Its common ion Cu²⁺ has an incomplete 3d⁹ subshell
x: An element counts as transition if its atom or one of its common ions has a partly filled d subshell. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, which qualifies copper. Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰, a complete subshell, so it does not qualify.

q: Which pair of ions has the same 3d electronic configuration?
x: Mn²⁺ (25 − 2 = 23 electrons) and Fe³⁺ (26 − 3 = 23 electrons) are both [Ar] 3d⁵. Cr³⁺ is 3d³ while Mn³⁺ is 3d⁴.

q: Which gaseous ion has the greatest number of unpaired electrons?
x: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ (5 unpaired). Co²⁺ is 3d⁷ (3), Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸ (2) and Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ (1). Unpaired electrons are greatest at d⁵.

q: Using μ = √(n(n + 2)) Bohr magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired electrons, the spin-only magnetic moment of a gaseous Fe²⁺ ion is about:
x: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ with 4 unpaired electrons: μ = √(4 × 6) = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM. 5.92 BM would be for 5 unpaired electrons (Fe³⁺).

q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a chromium atom in its ground state?
x: Cr is 3d⁵ 4s¹: five unpaired 3d electrons plus one unpaired 4s electron = 6. The expected but wrong 3d⁴4s² would give only 4.

q: Transition elements show variable oxidation states mainly because:
o: Their 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy and can both be used in bonding
They have very high first ionisation energies
Their outermost shell is completely filled
They have no electrons in the d subshell
x: The (n−1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, so different numbers of d electrons can be lost or shared along with the s electrons, giving several oxidation states.

q: The general outer electronic configuration of d-block elements is usually written as:
x: d-block elements are filling the (n−1)d subshell while the ns subshell holds one or two electrons. ns²np¹⁻⁶ is the p-block and ns¹⁻² alone is the s-block.

q: Which gaseous ion has no unpaired electrons?
x: Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, a full subshell with all electrons paired. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) and Ti³⁺ (3d¹) each have 1 unpaired electron, and V³⁺ (3d²) has 2.

q: How many electrons are present in the 3d subshell of a Co³⁺ ion (Co, Z = 27)?
x: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s². Forming Co³⁺ removes the two 4s electrons first and then one 3d electron, leaving 3d⁶. Taking all three from 3d would give 3d⁴ 4s².

q: In the complex K₃[Fe(CN)₆], the oxidation state and the coordination number of iron are:
x: Three K⁺ give the complex ion a charge of −3; with six CN⁻ ligands, x − 6 = −3, so Fe is +3. Six ligands each give one bond, so the coordination number is 6. +2 is iron in K₄[Fe(CN)₆], the usual mix-up.

q: The IUPAC name of K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is:
x: The complex ion is an anion, so the metal takes the -ate ending (ferrate). Fe: x − 6 = −4, so x = +2, written (II). 'Iron' without -ate is used only for neutral or cationic complexes; (III) would be K₃[Fe(CN)₆].

q: The IUPAC name of [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ is:
x: The complex ion [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ is a cation, so the metal keeps its ordinary name, copper; NH₃ is neutral, so Cu is +2. The -ate ending (cuprate) is used only when the complex is an anion, and (IV) comes from wrongly counting ammonia as charged.

q: A complex in which the central metal ion has coordination number 6, such as [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, has which geometry?
x: Six ligands around a central ion point to the corners of an octahedron (d²sp³ or sp³d² hybrid orbitals). Tetrahedral and square planar are the geometries for coordination number 4.

q: Ethylenediamine (en, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂) is a neutral bidentate ligand. In the complex ion [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺, the coordination number and oxidation state of cobalt are:
x: Each en forms two bonds, so 2 × 2 + 2 Cl = 6. Charge: x + 0 − 2 = +1, so x = +3. Counting each en as one bond gives 4; forgetting the Cl⁻ charges gives +1.

q: Which species can NOT act as a ligand?
x: A ligand must donate a lone pair to the metal ion. In NH₄⁺ the nitrogen lone pair is already used in bonding to the fourth H⁺, so none is left. NH₃, H₂O and Cl⁻ all have lone pairs.

q: The complex [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] exists as two different isomers (cis and trans). This shows that its geometry is:
x: With four ligands, a tetrahedral MA₂B₂ complex has only one arrangement because every corner is next to every other, so it cannot show cis–trans isomers. A square planar one has 'adjacent' and 'opposite' positions, giving two isomers. Octahedral needs six ligands.

q: Concentrated HCl is added to blue aqueous copper(II) sulphate. The solution turns yellow-green because of the formation of:
x: This is ligand exchange: the six H₂O ligands are replaced by four Cl⁻ ligands, [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O; the charge becomes 2 − 4 = −2. The deep-blue ammine complex forms with ammonia, not HCl.

q: How many ions are produced in water by one formula unit of [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃?
x: Only the ions outside the square bracket separate: [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ → [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ + 3Cl⁻, giving 4 ions. The NH₃ ligands stay bonded to cobalt, so counting them as separate particles gives 10.

q: In the blast furnace, haematite (Fe₂O₃) is reduced to iron mainly by:
x: Coke burns to CO₂, which is reduced by more hot coke to CO; CO then reduces the ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone is the flux, not the reducing agent.

q: Limestone is added to the blast furnace mainly to:
o: Increase the carbon content of the iron
Remove silica as calcium silicate slag
Supply oxygen for burning the coke
x: CaCO₃ decomposes to CaO, a basic oxide that combines with the acidic impurity SiO₂: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃, a molten slag that floats on the iron. The reducing agent is CO, not limestone.

q: Which order shows increasing carbon content?
x: Wrought iron is the purest commercial iron (about 0.1–0.25% C), steel has a moderate amount (about 0.25–2.5% C) and cast iron the most (about 2.5–4.5% C). Reversing the order is the common slip.

q: Dilute H₂SO₄ is added to yellow potassium chromate solution, and the colour changes to orange. Which statement is correct?
o: Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ forms because chromium is oxidised from +3 to +6
Green Cr³⁺ forms because chromium is reduced
Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ forms because chromium is oxidised from +6 to +7
Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ forms and chromium stays in the +6 state
x: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O is an acid–base equilibrium, not a redox change: Cr is +6 in both (x − 8 = −2; 2x − 14 = −2). Green Cr³⁺ appears only when dichromate is reduced by a reducing agent.

q: Acidified dichromate oxidises iron(II): Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. How many moles of Fe²⁺ are oxidised by 0.020 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻?
x: The ratio is 1 : 6, so 6 × 0.020 = 0.12 mol. Electron check: each Cr goes +6 → +3, so one Cr₂O₇²⁻ takes 6 electrons, one from each Fe²⁺. Using the 1 : 5 ratio of the KMnO₄ reaction gives 0.10 mol.

q: When KMnO₄ acts as an oxidising agent in acidic solution, the oxidation state of manganese changes from:
x: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, so Mn goes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons. +7 to +4 (MnO₂) happens in neutral or weakly alkaline solution, the usual mix-up.

q: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O. What volume of 0.020 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄ reacts exactly with 25.0 cm³ of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ sodium oxalate?
x: Oxalate = 0.0250 × 0.050 = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol; MnO₄⁻ = 2/5 × 1.25 × 10⁻³ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol; volume = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.020 = 0.025 dm³ = 25.0 cm³. Ignoring the 2 : 5 ratio gives 62.5 cm³, and inverting it gives 156 cm³.

q: No separate indicator is needed in titrations with acidified KMnO₄ because:
o: KMnO₄ changes from colourless to purple in acidic solution
Mn²⁺ ions form a brown precipitate at the end point
MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple while Mn²⁺ is almost colourless, so the first excess drop gives a pink colour
The CO₂ given off shows the end point
x: While the reducing agent remains, each drop of purple MnO₄⁻ is decolorised to nearly colourless Mn²⁺; once it is used up, one extra drop leaves a permanent pale pink. A brown MnO₂ precipitate means too little acid, not the end point.

q: In converting cast (pig) iron into steel, the main chemical change is:
o: Reduction of iron oxide by carbon monoxide
Adding more carbon to the iron
Oxidation of most of the carbon and of impurities such as Si, Mn and P
x: Steel making blows oxygen or air through molten pig iron, oxidising excess carbon to CO/CO₂ and Si, Mn and P to oxides that leave as slag; a set amount of carbon is then left or added. Reduction by CO is the blast-furnace step, not steel making.
